How to use AI in a small business office

Most advice about AI for small business is a list of forty tools. You do not need forty tools. You need one chore that stops landing on your desk.

Checked 2026-11-18. Menus in other products change, so a label may differ slightly on your screen.

Short answer: pick one repeated chore that involves reading something and writing something, such as chasing late invoices or sending a weekly update. Have AI prepare it, check its work for a few weeks, then move to the next chore. Do not start by buying a tool and looking for a use.

What AI is good at in an office

  • Writing from facts you give it: emails, reminders, summaries, replies.
  • Reading and sorting: pulling the amount and due date out of a document, deciding which rows on a list need attention.
  • Explaining: what changed in this week's figures compared with last week's.

What to keep a person on

  • Arithmetic. AI can get sums wrong while sounding certain. Totals should come from your software or a spreadsheet formula.
  • Anything it would have to guess. If the fact is not in front of it, it may make one up.
  • Decisions with consequences. Whether to chase a good customer, what to say in a dispute, who gets paid first.
  • The final look before something leaves the building.

How to find your first chore

Write down what you did last week that you also did the week before. For each one, ask:

  1. Does it happen at least every week?
  2. Does it follow the same steps each time?
  3. Is the information it needs written down somewhere, not in someone's head?
  4. Would a mistake be caught before it caused harm?

The chore with four yeses is your first one. In most offices it is invoice reminders, quote follow-ups, a weekly report or appointment confirmations.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with the hardest job. Start with the most boring one.
  • Pasting customer details into a free chat tool without knowing what it does with them. Check the privacy terms of anything you use for work.
  • Letting it send without review on day one.
  • Expecting it to know your business. It only knows what you tell it. Your rules, such as "never chase this customer", have to be written down for it.

Do you need to learn to program?

No. If you can explain a chore to a new member of staff, you can explain it to an AI tool. The skill that matters is being specific about what "done right" looks like.
